title: Control and Coordination
description: Grade 10 Biology: the nervous system, neurons and reflex action, the human brain, coordination in plants (tropisms and hormones), and hormones in animals.

topics.title: The Nervous System and Reflex Action
topics.concept:
Living organisms must respond to changes in their surroundings. A change that an organism responds to is a stimulus, and the reaction is a response. In animals, control and coordination are carried out by the nervous system and the hormonal (endocrine) system working together.

The basic unit of the nervous system is the nerve cell or neuron. A neuron has three parts: the dendrites (receive the message), the cell body and a long axon (carries the message away). Information travels along a neuron as an electrical impulse. The tiny gap between two neurons, across which the message passes using chemicals, is called a synapse.

A reflex action is a sudden, automatic and quick response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought — for example, pulling the hand away from a hot object. The pathway taken by the impulse during a reflex is the reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle). Reflex actions are controlled mainly by the spinal cord, so the response is fast and the brain is informed only afterwards. This protects us from harm in dangerous situations.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three parts of a neuron and the function of each.
examples.solution:
A neuron is built to receive and pass on impulses.

  • Dendrites — receive the message (impulse).
  • Cell body — processes it.
  • Axon — carries the impulse away to the next neuron or muscle.
examples.answer: Dendrites receive the impulse, the cell body processes it, and the axon carries it away.

examples.problem: Example 2: Trace the path of impulse in the reflex arc when you touch a hot plate.
examples.solution:
Recall the reflex arc sequence.

  • Receptor (skin) → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (arm muscle).
  • The muscle pulls the hand away.
examples.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle, which pulls the hand away.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are reflex actions important for survival?
examples.solution:
Reflexes act faster than conscious thought.

  • They give an immediate, automatic response.
  • This protects the body from harm before the brain has time to think.
examples.answer: Because they give an instant, automatic response that protects the body from harm before conscious thought can occur.

recap:
• A stimulus causes a response; the neuron is the unit of the nervous system (dendrite, cell body, axon).
  • Impulses travel electrically and cross a synapse chemically.
  • A reflex action is a quick, automatic response via the reflex arc (receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector).
  • Reflexes are controlled by the spinal cord for speed.

quiz.q: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
quiz.explanation: The neuron (nerve cell) is the basic unit of the nervous system.

quiz.q: A sudden, automatic response to a stimulus is called a:
quiz.explanation: A reflex action is a quick, automatic response controlled by the spinal cord.

topics.title: The Human Brain and Coordination
topics.concept:
The brain and spinal cord together form the central nervous system (CNS), while the nerves arising from them form the peripheral nervous system. The brain is protected by the bony skull and by fluid-filled membranes. It has three main parts:

  • Fore-brain (cerebrum) — the main thinking part. It controls voluntary actions, stores memory, and is the seat of intelligence, reasoning and the senses (sight, hearing, smell, etc.).
  • Mid-brain — connects the parts and controls some reflexes of the eyes.
  • Hind-brain — includes the cerebellum (controls posture, balance and precise voluntary movements such as walking and writing), the medulla (controls involuntary actions like heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, vomiting) and the pons.

The nervous system controls voluntary actions (under our will, e.g. talking, walking) through the cerebrum, and involuntary actions (not under our will, e.g. heartbeat, digestion) through the medulla. Nervous control is fast but its effect is usually short-lived; it works together with the slower, longer-lasting hormonal control to coordinate the body.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which part of the brain controls (a) thinking and memory, and (b) balance of the body?
examples.solution:
Different regions of the brain have different jobs.

  • (a) The fore-brain (cerebrum) controls thinking and memory.
  • (b) The cerebellum (in the hind-brain) controls balance and posture.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing?
examples.solution:
Vital involuntary actions are controlled automatically.

  • The medulla (in the hind-brain) controls heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure.
examples.answer: The medulla (medulla oblongata) controls involuntary actions like heartbeat and breathing.

examples.problem: Example 3: Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary actions with one example each.
examples.solution:
Compare control by will.

  • Voluntary — under our will, e.g. writing (controlled by cerebrum).
  • Involuntary — not under our will, e.g. heartbeat (controlled by medulla).
examples.answer: Voluntary actions are under our will (e.g. writing); involuntary actions are not (e.g. heartbeat).

recap:
• CNS = brain + spinal cord; brain protected by the skull.
  • Cerebrum (fore-brain) → thinking, memory, voluntary actions, senses.
  • Cerebellum → balance and posture; medulla → involuntary actions (heartbeat, breathing).
  • Nervous control is fast but short-lived; it works with slower hormonal control.

quiz.q: The part of the brain that controls balance and posture is the:
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum controls balance, posture and precise movements.

quiz.q: Heartbeat and breathing are involuntary actions controlled by the:
quiz.explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions like heartbeat and breathing.

topics.title: Coordination in Plants and Hormones in Animals
topics.concept:
Plants have no nervous system, yet they respond to stimuli — they coordinate using chemical substances (plant hormones). Plant responses are of two kinds:

  • Tropic movements (tropisms) — directional growth movements in response to a stimulus. In phototropism a shoot bends towards light; in geotropism (gravitropism) roots grow downward (towards gravity) and shoots upward; in hydrotropism roots grow towards water; in thigmotropism tendrils coil around a support.
  • Nastic movements — non-directional and quick, e.g. the folding of the leaves of the touch-me-not (Mimosa) on touch.

Plant hormones include auxin (promotes cell growth and is responsible for phototropism), gibberellin (stem growth), cytokinin (cell division), and abscisic acid (inhibits growth; causes wilting and falling of leaves).

In animals, the endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs. Important examples: the thyroid gland makes thyroxine (needs iodine; controls metabolism — its deficiency causes goitre); the pancreas makes insulin (controls blood sugar — its deficiency causes diabetes); the adrenal gland makes adrenaline (the ‘fight-or-flight’ hormone for emergencies); the pituitary makes growth hormone; and testes/ovaries make the sex hormones (testosterone/oestrogen) that bring about changes at puberty. Hormonal action is slower than nervous action but its effects last longer.

examples.problem: Example 1: A plant shoot bends towards light coming from a window. Name this response and the hormone responsible.
examples.solution:
Growth towards light is a tropism.

  • The response is phototropism.
  • It is caused by the hormone auxin, which makes the shaded side grow faster so the shoot bends towards light.
examples.answer: Phototropism; it is caused by the hormone auxin.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the hormone and gland involved in controlling blood sugar, and the disease caused by its deficiency.
examples.solution:
Blood sugar is controlled by a pancreatic hormone.

  • Hormone: insulin; gland: pancreas.
  • Its deficiency causes diabetes (high blood sugar).
examples.answer: Insulin, from the pancreas; its deficiency causes diabetes.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is iodine important in our diet, in terms of hormones?
examples.solution:
Iodine is needed to make a thyroid hormone.

  • The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine.
  • A lack of iodine causes goitre (swelling of the thyroid).
examples.answer: Iodine is needed by the thyroid to make thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre.

recap:
• Plants coordinate with hormones; tropisms (photo-, geo-, hydro-, thigmo-) are directional growth responses; nastic movements are non-directional (Mimosa).
  • Plant hormones: auxin (growth/phototropism), gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid.
  • Animal endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood: thyroxine (thyroid/iodine), insulin (pancreas → diabetes), adrenaline (adrenal), growth and sex hormones.
  • Hormonal control is slower but longer-lasting than nervous control.

quiz.q: The bending of a plant shoot towards light is called:
quiz.explanation: Growth towards light is phototropism, caused by auxin.

quiz.q: The 'fight-or-flight' hormone secreted during an emergency is:
quiz.explanation: Adrenaline, from the adrenal gland, prepares the body for emergencies.

questions.q: A change in the environment to which an organism responds is a:
questions.explanation: A stimulus is a change that an organism responds to.

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
questions.explanation: The neuron is the basic unit of the nervous system.

questions.q: The part of a neuron that receives impulses is the:
questions.explanation: Dendrites receive impulses; the axon carries them away.

questions.q: The microscopic gap between two neurons is the:
questions.explanation: A synapse is the gap across which the impulse passes chemically.

questions.q: A reflex action is mainly controlled by the:
questions.explanation: Reflex actions are controlled by the spinal cord for a quick response.

questions.q: The largest part of the human brain, responsible for thinking, is the:
questions.explanation: The cerebrum (fore-brain) controls thinking, memory and voluntary actions.

questions.q: Balance and posture of the body are controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum controls balance, posture and precise movements.

questions.q: Heartbeat and breathing are controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions like heartbeat and breathing.

questions.q: Plants coordinate their responses using:
questions.explanation: Plants have no nervous system; they coordinate using hormones.

questions.q: Roots growing downward into the soil is an example of:
questions.explanation: Growth in response to gravity is geotropism (gravitropism).

questions.q: The plant hormone responsible for phototropism is:
questions.explanation: Auxin causes the shoot to bend towards light (phototropism).

questions.q: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the:
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, which carries them to target organs.

questions.q: Insulin, which controls blood sugar, is secreted by the:
questions.explanation: Insulin is secreted by the pancreas; its deficiency causes diabetes.

questions.q: Goitre is caused by the deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Thyroxine needs iodine; lack of iodine causes goitre.

questions.q: Compared with nervous control, hormonal control is:
questions.explanation: Hormonal control acts more slowly than nervous control but its effects last longer.

questions.q: In a reflex like pulling away from a pin-prick, the brain learns about the event only AFTER the hand is withdrawn because:
options: The spinal cord handles the reflex quickly, then informs the brain
There are no nerves to the brain
questions.explanation: Reflexes are processed by the spinal cord for speed; the brain is informed afterwards.

questions.q: Auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light because it:
options: Collects on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer
questions.explanation: Auxin gathers on the shaded side, lengthening those cells, so the shoot bends towards light.

questions.q: Just before an exam, a student's heart races and palms sweat. This is mainly due to:
options: Adrenaline preparing the body for 'fight or flight'
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal gland prepares the body for stress (fight-or-flight).

questions.q: A person with very low thyroxine may feel tired and gain weight because thyroxine controls the body's:
questions.explanation: Thyroxine controls metabolic rate; too little slows metabolism, causing tiredness and weight gain.

questions.q: Why do plants rely on hormones rather than a nervous system for coordination?
options: They have no nerves or muscles; chemical signals diffuse to cause growth responses
Plants do not respond to stimuli
questions.explanation: Lacking nerves and muscles, plants coordinate through slow chemical (hormonal) signals that alter growth.

questions.q: Both the nervous system and hormones coordinate the body, which shows that the two systems:
options: Work together, each suited to fast or long-lasting control
questions.explanation: Fast nervous control and slower, lasting hormonal control complement each other to coordinate the body.
